newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP urges conservatives end euro row.
newsitem.headline: German FDP urges conservatives end euro row.

text.p: Germany's Free Democrats, junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government, on Monday called on the conservative Christian Democrats to resolve an internal dispute over the proposed single European currency.

FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle said persistent criticism of the euro by Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, a leading figure in the Christian Social Union (CSU), could harm the coalition in the long run.
The CSU is the sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).
Stoiber has insisted that economic stability criteria be met fully before the euro is launched, a strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty on monetary union that Kohl and CDU leaders reject.
"It would be good if the CDU and CSU could reach an agreement," said Hermann Otto Solms, FDP parliamentary leader.
Wolfgang Gerhardt, the FDP chairman, said Stoiber was only stirring uncertainty with his remarks rather than creating more stability, which he says he wants.

Gerhardt said the FDP wanted to ensure that Germany's deficit did not exceed the reference level of three percent of gross domestic product set in the Maastricht treaty but added, "No one could say the euro would be less stable if the deficit is slightly above this level."
In Berlin, CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said it was wrong to pit stability criteria against the time schedule for the introduction of the euro.
Hintze said that the euro would start on time in 1999 and the debate about the time schedule versus the stability criteria was counterproductive.
"The stability criteria as the anchor of the European economic and monetary union (EMU) will remain firmly in place and are irrevocable," Hintze said before a meeting of CDU leaders in Berlin.
He added: "The euro will start on time."
